The Mann–Whitney U test

Work through the biological example, calculations and interpretation in the lesson. The complete infographic at the end is a visual recap of the material covered here.

Learning goals. By the end, you should be able to identify an independent-groups design, choose between a t-test and Mann–Whitney, calculate U in a small example, interpret a p-value and an appropriate distributional effect size, and run the analysis in R.
1 · Biological question

What are we comparing?

A researcher asks whether exposure to a sub-inhibitory antibiotic concentration is associated with a change in bacterial biofilm production.

Control group

Independent cultures grown without antibiotic. Each biological replicate contributes one biofilm measurement.

Antibiotic group

Different independent cultures grown with a sub-inhibitory antibiotic concentration. Each replicate contributes one measurement.

The outcome is biofilm biomass, measured for example by a validated crystal-violet assay (optical density) or image-based biomass measurement. The experimental unit is the independently grown culture/well, not repeated technical readings from the same culture.

Biological caution. Antibiotics can sometimes stimulate biofilm formation at sub-inhibitory concentrations, but this is organism-, drug- and dose-dependent. The example asks a research question; it does not assume the treatment must increase biofilm.
2 · Choosing the method

Why Mann–Whitney instead of a t-test?

Use a t-test when:

  • The biological question concerns a difference in group means.
  • Within-group distributions are approximately normal, with no strong outliers; for unequal variances, use Welch’s t-test.

Consider Mann–Whitney when:

  • The outcome is ordinal, or a rank-based comparison is the scientific target.
  • Normality is doubtful (for example, with small samples or strong skewness/outliers).
  • You want to compare the relative ordering of observations between two independent groups, not their means.

Important: skewness alone does not automatically make Mann–Whitney the right test. Choose according to the biological question, design, sample size and data. Welch’s t-test does not require equal variances.

When can we describe the result as a difference in medians?

Example A — similar shapes, shifted location. A difference in medians is a reasonable description.

Example B — different shapes and spreads. Describe a difference between distributions; do not reduce it automatically to a difference in medians.

Key point: The median interpretation is appropriate when the distributions have similar shapes and spreads and differ mainly in location.

3 · Before testing

Assumptions and hypotheses

  • Two independent groups (for example, different cultures or biological replicates).
  • The outcome is at least ordinal, so observations can be ranked.
  • Observations are independent; technical replicates do not replace independent biological replicates.
  • For a location/median interpretation only: the two distributions should have similar shapes and spreads. This is not required for the general distributional comparison.

Hypotheses

Two-sided alternative (used in this worked example):

H₀: The two population distributions are identical.
H₁: The two population distributions differ.

One-sided alternative (illustrative only): if the biological question, specified before collecting or examining the data, is whether sub-inhibitory antibiotic exposure tends to produce higher biofilm measurements:

H₀: P(A > C) = P(A < C).
H₁: P(A > C) > P(A < C).

Here A is a randomly selected antibiotic observation and C is a randomly selected control observation. The alternative says that an antibiotic value is more likely to exceed a control value than to fall below it.

A one-sided test is justified only by a genuinely directional research question set in advance. It should not be chosen after seeing which group has the larger values.

4 · How the statistic works

Rank the observations and calculate U

Pool all observations and rank them from smallest to largest. Mann–Whitney uses the ranks rather than the original measurement values.

GroupObservations (in ascending order)Ranks
Control0.8 · 1.0 · 1.1 · 1.2 · 1.3 · 1.41 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6
Antibiotic1.6 · 1.8 · 1.9 · 2.0 · 2.2 · 2.47 · 8 · 9 · 10 · 11 · 12

Each group is shown on its own row for easier presentation. The ranks are assigned after pooling all 12 observations and ordering them from smallest to largest.

Rank sums: RC = 21 and RA = 57. Each U counts cross-group pairwise orderings for one group.

UC = RC − nC(nC+1)/2 = 21 − (6×7)/2 = 0
UA = RA − nA(nA+1)/2 = 57 − (6×7)/2 = 36
UC + UA = nCnA = 36; report the smaller U = 0.

Here all antibiotic values exceed all control values: every one of the 36 antibiotic–control pairs favours the antibiotic group. With ties, average ranks are assigned and the usual U interpretation gives half-credit to tied pairs.

5 · P-value and inference

Exact test for this example

With six observations in each group and complete separation (U = 0), the observed result is as extreme as possible. Under H₀, every allocation of 6 of the 12 pooled ranks to one group is equally likely.

Number of allocations = C(12,6) = 924
Two-sided exact p = 2 / C(12,6) = 2 / 924 = 0.00216

This shortcut is for complete separation with no ties. For other U values, the exact p-value is calculated from the null distribution of U.

Why can fewer than four observations per group not give p < 0.05?

For equal group sizes, the smallest possible two-sided exact p-value occurs with complete separation:

pmin = 2 / C(2n,n)
  • n = 3 per group: 2 / C(6,3) = 2/20 = 0.10. Even perfect separation cannot reach 0.05.
  • n = 4 per group: 2 / C(8,4) = 2/70 = 0.0286. A p-value below 0.05 is now possible.

This is due to the limited number of possible rank allocations, not a software limitation. With unequal group sizes, the minimum attainable p-value depends on both sample sizes.

Normal approximation (large samples)

For larger samples, the distribution of U under the null hypothesis can be approximated by a normal distribution. The quantities below are the mean (μU) and standard deviation (σU) of the null distribution of U, not the sample mean and sample SD of the biological measurements.

Mean of U under H0: μU = n1 n22 = 18
Standard deviation of U under H0: σU = √ n1 n2 (n1 + n2 + 1)12 = √39 ≈ 6.24

For this example, U = 0. Using a continuity correction of 0.5:

Z = U − μU + 0.5σU = 0 − 18 + 0.56.24 = −2.80
Z is compared with the standard normal distribution, N(0, 1).
Two-sided p ≈ 0.0051

The Z statistic is compared with the standard normal distribution, N(0, 1), and the corresponding tail area gives the p-value. It does not follow a Student's t distribution and therefore has no degrees of freedom. A t distribution with degrees of freedom is used in procedures such as the t-test, not in this normal approximation to the Mann–Whitney U statistic.

The exact p-value (0.00216) is preferred for this small example. The normal approximation is close, but not identical. With ties, a tie correction is needed for the variance. There is no universal sample-size cut-off at which the approximation suddenly becomes valid.

R example: exact test and normal approximation

Now run the same biofilm data in R. First request the exact test; then request the normal approximation with a continuity correction. The code runs in your browser using WebR.

R output will appear here.

How to read the R output

R labels its reported test statistic W. For the two-sample test, the numerical value reported is the first group's rank sum minus n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 — that is, the corresponding U statistic for the first group. With the antibiotic group supplied first, R reports W = 36:

UA = W = 36
UC = nAnC − UA = 36 − 36 = 0
U = min(UA, UC) = 0

The other group's statistic is UC = 36 − 36 = 0, so the smaller value is U = 0, matching our hand calculation. The exact two-sided p-value is approximately 0.00216. The normal approximation with continuity correction gives approximately 0.0051. Both lead to rejection of H0 at α = 0.05, but the exact result is preferable for these small samples.

Teaching point: R labels the returned statistic W, but for the two-sample test its value is the U statistic for the first group. Our hand calculation reports both group-specific U values and then uses the smaller one.

Understand the output

  • R labels the rank-sum statistic as W.
  • For the antibiotic group here, W = 57.
  • Its corresponding U is W − n(n+1)/2 = 57 − 21 = 36; the smaller U is 0.
  • The exact two-sided p-value is approximately 0.0022.
If WebR cannot load because of a network restriction, copy the same code into R or RStudio. The statistical lesson and exercises remain usable.
